project.name: ChenDB
project.what: A relational database engine written from scratch in Python, plus a React web app (the Visual Database Explorer) that shows what the engine is doing while it does it. Monorepo: engine/ + visualizer/.

workflow_conventions.branching: One branch per milestone: milestone-N-<slug>, branched from MASTER (not from the previous milestone branch). Stacking caused a real problem once: PR #2 was based on the M1 branch, and because that branch was kept alive after #1 merged, GitHub never retargeted #2 — it merged into the M1 branch instead of master and needed a manual fix-up merge. Always branch from master and always merge with --delete-branch.
workflow_conventions.pr: One PR per milestone, opened with `gh pr create`. STANDING AUTHORIZATION from the user: merge each milestone yourself as soon as it is done — do not ask. Use `gh pr merge N --merge --delete-branch`.
workflow_conventions.versioning: engine.__version__ and pyproject version track the milestone: MILESTONE = major * 10 + minor, so 1.6.0 is Milestone 16. Bump BOTH, and nothing else — engine/server/app.py imports MILESTONE from engine rather than holding its own copy, which is exactly why it stopped drifting. Then: run `make types` in the SAME commit (FastAPI puts the version in the OpenAPI document, and CI diffs the committed copy), update the exact number in tests/integration/test_api.py, and if the milestone added no engine capability add it to MILESTONES_WITHOUT_ENGINE_FEATURES with a reason. AND: editing a DOCSTRING anywhere under engine/server/ also requires `make types` in the same commit. Pydantic uses a model's docstring as its JSON-schema description and FastAPI uses a route function's docstring as the operation description, so prose changes there move docs/openapi.json. This is not obvious and it cost a red CI run.
workflow_conventions.verified_means: `make ci` (lint, typecheck, both test suites, every example on a bare interpreter) AND, since Milestone 17, a differential campaign: `scripts/differential.py --seeds 0:5000` clean. For anything touching the WASM build, seen working in a real browser — the M15/M16 bugs were all invisible to the test suite. A new guard is not verified until you have watched it FAIL against the bug it exists for.
workflow_conventions.honesty_rule: Features that do not exist are ABSENT from the API and HIDDEN in the UI — never stubbed, never greyed out. engine/server/app.py:FEATURES drives which visualizer workspace tabs render.
workflow_conventions.handover: handover.json goes through a branch and a PR like everything else. Two commits in one session went straight to master; that was a deviation, not the convention. Refresh it as work lands, and ALWAYS before the context window fills — see the standing instruction to update it and then say it is safe to /compact.
workflow_conventions.user_facing_text: NO EM DASHES. Not in user-facing text, not in prose, not in docstrings, not in comments, not in the README or docs. 1,773 were removed; the 38 that remain are all a standalone '—' used as a PLACEHOLDER for an absent value (an empty buffer frame, a WAL record with no transaction, formatBytes of NaN, a 'not applicable' column in an ASCII diagram) plus the guard that discusses the character itself. Use a comma, colon, semicolon, full stop or parentheses instead. ALSO: user-facing text may not name a NUMBERED milestone. A milestone number means nothing to somebody using the explorer. The TopBar version badge says 'milestone' without a number and is deliberately allowed. Both rules are enforced by visualizer/src/test/uiText.test.ts, which strips comments first so a comment may still say 'the buffer pool arrived in Milestone 7' (that is documentation of history) while a tooltip may not.

the_bugs_it_found: a non-boolean WHERE matched nothing and said nothing. is_true was `value is True`, so `5 is True` is False and a value that was never a condition looked exactly like a row that failed one. SUM over TEXT returned a concatenation ('abd'), typed TEXT.

NaN and infinity were storable and broke ORDER BY (genuinely unsorted), MIN/MAX (seed never displaced), and index scans — engine/index/key.py orders NaN above +inf while the evaluator says NaN > 398.0 is false, so an index scan and a seq scan returned DIFFERENT ROWS for one predicate.
a FLOAT index bound rounded an integer literal and was absorbed anyway, so f = 2^63-1 and f > 2^63-1 were both INVERTED by the presence of an index.
WHERE id = 3 AND id = 2 returned the row with id 2. _bounds_for folded two equalities by assignment rather than intersection and marked both absorbed. Latent until PRIMARY KEY gave id an index.

milestone_18.shipped: LEFT / RIGHT / FULL OUTER JOIN, end to end. Parser accepts the three sides (OUTER is noise); JoinKind gains is_outer/preserves_left/preserves_right; BoundJoin and LogicalJoin carry the kind; PhysicalJoin base class with preserve_left/preserve_right; NULL extension in both operators. The M17 generator emits outer joins in ~40% of generated joins.
milestone_18.why_the_executor_was_easy: NULL extension is FREE, and it is a consequence of Milestone 13's row layout. Every row below the topmost join is already the full width of the FROM with the unjoined tables left None, so a left row that found no partner has simply never had the right side copied into it — emitting it unchanged IS the extension. M13 paid for that layout in row width; this is the refund.
the_planner_was_the_milestone: ON and WHERE are no longer one pool. `ON ... AND o.total > 200` decides what MATCHES; the same predicate in the WHERE removes the preserved rows. Both correct, different queries. An outer join's ON never enters the pool: not pushed down, not pulled up, not merged.

Pushdown is conditional in one direction. _null_supplied computes which scan positions an outer join can NULL-extend; those get no pushdown. Pushing into the PRESERVED side is still legal and still happens. RIGHT is why the set is computed by walking the chain — it null-extends everything to its left.

An outer join is a BARRIER. _plan_chain lets consecutive inner joins form a segment the System-R search orders freely; an outer join closes it, runs where written, and becomes ONE OPAQUE RELATION. Exactly the right freedom, and it falls out: the search CAN commute that relation (an inner join's inputs may be swapped) but can NEVER re-associate into it.

Build-side selection survives. preserve_left/preserve_right describe the PHYSICAL inputs, so swapping an outer join's sides and flipping the flags gives an identical output row — RowLayout fixes column positions by written order. Only the order relative to other joins is constrained.

_join_cardinality got a floor (a preserved row appears whether it matched or not) and that exposed something worse: it read POSITIONS INTO THE SHARED POOL, which an outer join contributes nothing to. Every outer join was costed as a CROSS PRODUCT — 60 rows joined to 300 estimated at 18,000 instead of 90. It now takes the terms themselves.
milestone_18.the_bug_the_fuzzer_found: HashJoin emitted an unmatched probe row when its bucket was EMPTY. Wrong condition: a hash join hashes the equality and re-checks the residual per pair, so a probe row can hash into a FULL bucket and be rejected by every candidate in it. `FULL JOIN ... ON a.id = b.aid AND b.aid > 0` lost two of three rows. Nine hand-written FULL JOIN cases all had a bare equality for their ON and missed it; the generator found it on the first run, because a third of its outer joins carry an extra term on the null-supplied side. Fixed with a _probe_matched flag.
milestone_18.what_is_given_up: No reordering across an outer join — an inner join written after one cannot move before it, even where legal. PostgreSQL recovers those with min_lefthand/min_righthand per SpecialJoinInfo; that is a milestone of its own. EXPLAIN says so rather than hiding it. Also no outer-join simplification: `a LEFT JOIN b ON ... WHERE b.x = 5` is provably an inner join and ChenDB does not rewrite it.
milestone_18.verified: make ci green; 160,000 differential pairs clean with outer joins in the mix.

milestone_19.shipped: Outer-join simplification. engine/optimizer/nullability.py proves that a predicate cannot be TRUE once a table's columns are all NULL; _simplify_outer_joins in engine/optimizer/rules.py uses that to reduce LEFT/RIGHT/FULL to the smaller join they really are. Plus JoinKind.of, the inverse of preserves_left/preserves_right, which is what makes the rewrite one line applied twice.
milestone_19.the_analysis: Abstract interpretation over SETS of truth values, not strictness flags. Every column of a NULL-supplied table is known NULL, everything else is ANY, and the result is pushed through SQL's own truth tables. TRUE absent from the set is a proof TRUE is impossible. Sound because every rule returns a SUPERSET, which is why an unrecognised node returns ANY: a new AST node then costs a missed rewrite, never a wrong answer. Written out rather than done with a strictness flag because IS NULL is not strict (it goes TRUE on exactly the invented rows, the anti-join idiom) and neither is OR (NULL OR TRUE is TRUE, so an OR rejects only when both sides do).
what_counts_as_evidence: The ON of any LATER join in the chain that does not preserve its left input, because such a join discards an accumulated row its ON rejects. INNER is one, and so is RIGHT. That makes `a LEFT JOIN b ON ... JOIN c ON b.k = c.k` an inner join with no WHERE at all.
NOT the outer join's own ON. It decides which rows MATCH, and the non-matching rows are precisely the ones it preserves. This is the bug the rule is one step away from at all times.
NOT an earlier join's ON (it ran before the NULLs existed) and NOT HAVING (it runs after grouping).
The chain is walked OUTERMOST FIRST so a join reduced this pass counts as its reduced kind for the ones inside it. One pass, not a fixed point.
milestone_19.the_second_bug: Measuring the milestone found join_selectivity passing ROW COUNTS where DISTINCT COUNTS belong. 50 users joined to 4,000 orders was estimated at 50 * 4000 / 4000 = 50, the size of the wrong side, off by 80x and compounding to 6,400x on three tables. distinct_join_selectivity had spelled the right formula since Milestone 6 and NOTHING had ever called it. Wired up as _joined_distinct_counts in engine/planner/physical.py; no existing test needed to change. It hid because Milestone 18's outer-join floor rescued RIGHT and FULL by accident, so only half the cases were visibly wrong.
milestone_19.measured: 50 users, 4,000 orders, median of 25 runs, `WHERE o.total = 42` over a LEFT JOIN: 19.4 ms -> 13.4 ms with no index (1.5x), 19.4 ms -> 0.47 ms with an index on orders.total (41x). The 41x is the index doing the work and the rewrite is what let the query reach it.

the_two_rules: VALIDITY: a subset is only one a plan could hold if every outer join whose table it contains also has its min_left inside it. Half an outer join is not a relation: {b, c} is impossible when b exists only because a LEFT-JOIN b ran.

ELIGIBILITY: an outer join may run when its min_left is present AND every outer join written before it has run. Outer joins keep their order relative to each other; the inner ones are what gained freedom.

architecture_invariants.consequence: `import engine` works with zero third-party packages installed. Keep it that way.

key_design_decisions.diagnostics: Events are frozen dataclasses with `category`/`level` as ClassVars. ALWAYS guard emits with the cached flag: `if tracer.storage: tracer.emit(XEvent(...))`. Measured 8.5ns guarded vs 296ns unguarded (35x) because Python builds the argument before the call. NULL_TRACER is the no-op default.
key_design_decisions.snapshot_consistency: Diagnostics endpoints: take the ManagedDatabase lock, copy immutable dataclasses, RELEASE, then map to Pydantic. Never serialize under the lock.
key_design_decisions.ws_backpressure: Per-connection bounded asyncio.Queue; on overflow drop OLDEST and report count in a `dropped` frame. Subscription.offer() runs on the engine thread and only calls loop.call_soon_threadsafe — it must never block.
key_design_decisions.ast_spans: Every AST node carries node_id + SourceSpan(start, end, line, column). Node.children()/attributes() are generic via dataclasses.fields. INVARIANT: a node field must be a scalar, a Node, or a FLAT tuple — never a tuple of tuples (that made InsertStatement values invisible; fixed with the ValuesRow node). Guarded by test_no_node_hides_children_inside_a_nested_tuple.
key_design_decisions.ast_wire_format: The AST crosses the wire FLAT (nodes[] + root_ids[]), not nested — recursive Pydantic makes bad OpenAPI, and the UI needs random access by node_id anyway.
key_design_decisions.parse_errors: analyze_sql() never raises; it returns ParseOutcome with partial tokens + statements + error. POST /parse always returns 200 — invalid SQL is a result, not a failed request. UnsupportedSqlError (subclass of ParseError) is used for valid-SQL-not-implemented-yet and names a milestone.
key_design_decisions.typescript_types: visualizer/src/types/api.ts is GENERATED from OpenAPI by scripts/generate_api_types.py. Never hand-edit. Re-run after any schema change.
key_design_decisions.monaco: Imported from 'monaco-editor/esm/vs/editor/editor.api' (NOT 'monaco-editor') — the latter pulls every built-in language and roughly triples the bundle. Custom 'chendb-sql' Monarch grammar with only the keywords the engine's lexer knows. loader.config({monaco}) points @monaco-editor/react at the local copy instead of a CDN.
key_design_decisions.three_valued_logic: NULL is *unknown*, not false. Only an exact True passes a WHERE (is_true()). FALSE AND NULL is FALSE; TRUE OR NULL is TRUE. IsNullTest is a distinct AST node, never BinaryOp(EQ, x, NULL). Truth tables are pinned exhaustively in tests/unit/test_expression.py — getting them wrong gives silently wrong answers.
key_design_decisions.volcano_model: Explicit open()/next()/close() rather than Python generators, because it is the real volcano interface, operators must be inspectable while suspended, and pausing between calls must be trivial. Cost is a method call per row per operator; vectorised execution (batches of ~2048) is the big idea deliberately given up.
key_design_decisions.step_mode: StepController blocks the engine thread on a threading.Condition at checkpoints. Cancellation RAISES inside the engine thread at the next checkpoint so operators unwind through close(). 'Run until page read' works by registering the controller as a diagnostics SINK — storage knows nothing about stepping. A paused execution holds its database lock; cancel() deliberately needs no lock. ExecutionStore.reap() cancels idle executions on every store operation (no background timer).
key_design_decisions.catalog_bootstrap: The system tables' own schemas are COMPILED IN (engine/catalog/system.py), not stored — otherwise decoding chendb_tables would require reading chendb_tables. Unlike PostgreSQL, chendb_tables holds NO row about itself: that would be two sources of truth for where the catalog lives. System descriptors are synthesised from the compiled schemas plus the meta pointers. Table ids 1-2 are system, users start at 100, 3-99 reserved for future system tables.
key_design_decisions.catalog_cache: Lookups cached in memory per open database; a miss is O(tables)+O(columns) page reads. Coherence by single writer: every mutation goes through Catalog and updates the cache in the same call. CRITICAL: when a table's heap extends, its chendb_tables row must be rewritten — a stale last_page makes a reopened database append into the MIDDLE of the chain, silently.
key_design_decisions.index_key_encoding: M5 index keys use an ORDER-PRESERVING encoding (big-endian, sign-flipped) so a comparison is one memcmp, not two struct.unpack calls. It is a SECOND encoding, separate from serialization/types.py, which stays little-endian for records. Every key carries a 1-byte tag: 0x00 minus-infinity, 0x01 NULL, 0x02 value. The tag is what orders NULL (below every value, SQLite-style) and what gives internal nodes a sentinel first separator, removing the need for a 'leftmost child' header field.
key_design_decisions.index_entry_sort_key: B+ tree entries sort by (key, record_id), not key alone, so every entry is unique. That makes duplicates splittable anywhere and makes deleting one row's entry a descent instead of a scan. PostgreSQL 12 did the same. They compare as a PAIR, not as concatenated bytes — concatenating reintroduces the prefix problem and would need an escape-and-terminate layer, which is also why M5 indexes ONE column.
key_design_decisions.no_node_merging: The tree never merges on delete: an entry is removed, the leaf is left underfull, an emptied leaf stays linked. Deliberate — merging needs sibling+parent locking that only breaks under load. Space is reused in place by later inserts (test_space_from_deletions_is_reused_in_place) but never returned to the file.
key_design_decisions.split_point: plan_split() balances by BYTES then clamps to the range where both halves fit. By count breaks on variable-width TEXT keys. The clamp range is provably non-empty: a node overflows once, so total <= capacity + one entry, and one entry always fits on a page alone.
key_design_decisions.rule_based_access_path: Access-path choice is RULE-based in M5 and knowingly wrong above ~5% selectivity — benchmarks/index_vs_scan.py shows the index 3.8x SLOWER at 70% selectivity, because it does one random heap read per matching row. That is the evidence M6's cost model is built to act on; do NOT 'fix' it with a hand-tuned threshold.
key_design_decisions.null_and_range_bounds: A range bounded only from above must anchor its low end at SMALLEST_VALUE_KEY (b'\x02'), or it sweeps up the NULL keys — and no comparison is ever true for NULL. See _bounds_for() in engine/executor/engine.py.
key_design_decisions.btree_view_is_hand_drawn: The B+ tree view is hand-drawn SVG, not d3-hierarchy and not React Flow. d3's tidy-tree assumes uniform node widths and only draws tree edges; a B+ tree node is a variable-width row of cells and the leaf chain is not a tree edge. Placing boxes directly is less code than bending d3 to it, and adds no dependency.
key_design_decisions.cost_constants_are_measured: engine/optimizer/cost.py's constants are FITTED to benchmarks/index_vs_scan.py, not copied from PostgreSQL. PostgreSQL makes CPU 100x cheaper than a page read; here CPU_TUPLE_COST is 0.15 against PAGE_COST 1.0, because a page read hits the OS cache while a row costs interpreted Python. Copying PostgreSQL's ratio made the model refuse the index at 0.3% selectivity where it still wins by 80x. The fit is ~18.9 us per cost unit across a 650x range AND across both access paths — that second part is what stops the planner mis-weighting one path against the other. Re-measure when Milestone 7 lands.
key_design_decisions.statistics_not_persisted: No chendb_stats table and no format version 4. A statistic has no correctness consequence (a wrong one is a slow query, never a wrong answer), the interesting failure is STALENESS, and PostgreSQL persists only because rescanning a terabyte at startup is impossible — a reason that does not apply here. Gathered lazily on first plan, refreshed by ANALYZE, staleness detected by comparing the page-write counter.
key_design_decisions.stale_statistics_are_used: Deliberately. A slightly old estimate beats none, and recomputing per insert would cost a full scan per row. Staleness is REPORTED instead — in EXPLAIN, in PlanModel.statistics.stale, and as a warning in the UI.
key_design_decisions.physical_nodes_are_data: PhysicalIndexScan holds an index NAME and key bounds, not a BPlusTree. materialise() turns a plan into operators as a separate step, which is what lets EXPLAIN cost a query it never runs and lets the API serialise a plan outside the engine lock.
key_design_decisions.every_alternative_is_reported: PlanAlternativeEvent fires once per candidate, chosen or not, and PlanModel.alternatives carries all of them with rejected_because. A planner that reports only its answer cannot be checked.
key_design_decisions.disabled_paths_are_penalised: PlannerOptions turns a path off by adding DISABLE_COST = 1e10, not by removing it — PostgreSQL's disable_cost trick — because a query with every path disabled must still produce a plan.
key_design_decisions.stepping_starts_at_execution: StepController.arm() gates checkpoints until the operator tree opens. Planning reads pages (gathering statistics scans the table), so without it the first dozen steps of every stepped query were the planner counting rows. Cancellation is NOT gated. EXPLAIN is how you inspect the part that is skipped.
key_design_decisions.buffer_pool_has_no_pin_counts: ChenDB's pool copies OUT of a frame on read and INTO it on write, so a caller's Page is independent and eviction can never invalidate one. That removes the need for pin counts entirely — and no caller had to change. A textbook pool lends a pointer into the frame and requires pinning; that is the right design once there are concurrent readers (Milestone 10). Pin counts that are always zero would be ceremony, so there are none, and BufferPoolEvent has no pin_count field despite the planned schema naming one.
key_design_decisions.validate_is_off_the_read_path: Page.validate() is O(slots) — 13.3us on a full 4 KiB page, measured, against 103ns for the CRC32. Running it per read made the buffer pool nearly worthless. from_bytes now runs validate_header() (O(1)) only; the full slot walk is explicit, for the inspector and tests. PostgreSQL draws the same line. If a test needs the strong check, call page.validate() directly.
key_design_decisions.on_is_not_where: For an INNER join, `a JOIN b ON p` and `a, b WHERE p` mean the same thing, so plan_select pools them and pushes each single-table conjunct to its scan. For an OUTER join every part of that fails, so its ON is kept out of the pool and applied at the join. Three placements of the same predicate — pushed below, at the join, above the join — are three different queries, and EXPLAIN shows which.
key_design_decisions.an_outer_join_is_a_barrier: The System-R search's licence to reorder is that an inner join is commutative and associative. _plan_chain therefore lets consecutive inner joins form a segment the search orders freely, and an outer join closes the segment and becomes one OPAQUE relation. Opaque is exactly right and costs nothing to enforce: the search can commute that relation with others but has no way to reach inside it, so it can never build a ⟕ (b ⨝ c) from (a ⟕ b) ⨝ c. The cost is that an inner join written after an outer one cannot move before it.
key_design_decisions.null_extension_is_free: Milestone 13 made a row's layout the written order of the FROM, always, and paid for it in row width. That is what makes NULL extension free: an unmatched left row already has None in the right side's slots, because nothing ever wrote them. Emitting it unchanged IS the extension, and the mirror holds for the right side.
key_design_decisions.a_registry_excuses_errors_not_values: The differential registry can record 'ChenDB refuses what SQLite accepts' and never 'both returned rows and the rows differed'. An error is a categorical outcome a human has already reasoned about; a wrong row is what the tester exists to find. Entries match on outcomes only — no SQL, no seed — so there is no known-failing-seeds list, which is the line between knowledge and an undiagnosed bug.
key_design_decisions.an_outer_join_may_not_be_one: Milestone 19's rule changes what a join IS, not how it runs, and it saves nothing by itself: an inner join and an outer join over the same inputs cost the same. The whole return is second-hand, through two prohibitions Milestone 18 correctly imposed. Predicate pushdown may not cross into a NULL-supplied side and the join-order search may not cross an outer join; an inner join is subject to neither. That is why it lives in rules.py rather than inline: it pays off in parts of the planner it never mentions.
key_design_decisions.soundness_defaults_to_declining: engine/optimizer/nullability.py returns ANY for any expression it does not recognise, so a rewrite fires only on the ABSENCE of TRUE from the possible set. Every new AST node is therefore safe by default. Defaulting the other way would mean each future node silently licences a rewrite until somebody notices, and the failure mode is not a crash: it is FEWER ROWS, quietly, with nothing downstream to blame.
key_design_decisions.estimates_are_checked_against_reality: tests/unit/test_estimates.py is the first test in this project that compares a planner estimate against the number of rows the query actually returns. Its absence is exactly how join_selectivity divided by row counts instead of distinct counts for fourteen milestones: every test around it checked that the arithmetic was the arithmetic somebody had written down. A bad estimate never produces a wrong answer, so this suite is the only thing that can fail when one appears. Counted with COUNT(*), never len(rows), because execute_script stops at DEFAULT_MAX_ROWS = 10,000.
key_design_decisions.skew_and_shape_are_different_problems: Skew lives in the HEAD of a distribution and shape lives in the TAIL, which is why pg_statistic keeps two structures and Milestone 20 copied the division. most_common answers 'how many rows have exactly this value'; the histogram answers 'how many are below this bound'. Equi-depth rather than equi-width is the choice that makes the second worth having: equal-width buckets over a clustered column describe empty space in detail and put every row in one bucket.
key_design_decisions.a_pooled_conjunct_remembers_where_it_cam: Milestone 13 pooled the WHERE with every inner join's ON, on the true observation that for an inner join the two are interchangeable. They are not interchangeable in the PRESENCE of an outer join: an ON below one runs before its NULL-extension and a WHERE runs after. Pooling discards exactly the fact needed to protect them differently, so plan_select now carries a parallel `origins` list and _null_supplied takes `before=`. Any future rule that reasons about where a predicate may be applied needs the origin, not just the tables.
key_design_decisions.an_outer_join_constrains_rather_than_fre: Milestone 18 made an outer join a barrier that closed a search segment. Milestone 22 makes it a constraint the one search checks: min_left says what must already be joined, validity says which subsets are reachable at all. The barrier was the safe over-approximation and cost real plans; the constraint is the same safety with a proof attached. Anything added to the join search from now on must satisfy _is_valid, or it will cost subplans no executor could produce.

starlette's TestClient websocket transport is UNBOUNDED, so the WS drop policy can never be exercised through it. That policy is unit-tested directly in tests/unit/test_ws_backpressure.py.
GET /databases/{db} calls db.count(), which itself does page reads — do not use it to measure page reads across an operation unless the database has no table.

Ruff N818 is globally ignored: exception class names (DatabaseNotFound, InvalidDatabaseId, ...) are returned verbatim in the API error envelope and asserted on by clients.
Crash tests SIGKILL a child process on purpose. Never 'fix' them to close cleanly — a cooperative shutdown flushes the very buffers under test.
Milestone 1 persists the schema as JSON across a CHAIN of SCHEMA pages (a 380-byte descriptor does not fit one 256-byte page). Milestone 4 replaces this with real system tables.
Small page sizes (256) are used throughout the tests deliberately: 4 rows fill a page, so chaining/compaction are exercised by a handful of inserts.

Response models: prefer required-but-nullable over optional. A Pydantic field with a default (default_factory=list, = None) becomes `?` in the generated TS even though the server always sends it, which forces `?? []` at every call site. Drop the default and use `X | None` instead.

Operator.open() contains checkpoints, so it must sit INSIDE the try block in _execute_select — otherwise cancelling during open propagates instead of returning a partial result. Fixed once; test_cancelling_unwinds_the_operator_tree guards it.

Column `position` is stored in chendb_columns and is load-bearing: a heap scan returns PHYSICAL order, not column order, and they diverge once a deleted slot is reused. _load_schema sorts by position and rejects non-contiguous positions as corruption.
File format v2: version-1 files are rejected on open, deliberately. Delete old *.chendb files after pulling M4.
GET /databases/{db} now scans the catalog, so it CAUSES page reads. Do not use it to measure page reads across an operation without calibrating against two back-to-back probes.

Milestone 5 will need FORMAT VERSION 3 (meta page gains catalog_indexes_first/last). Bump FORMAT_VERSION in engine/storage/constants.py, extend META_HEADER_FORMAT in engine/storage/meta.py, and update _meta_header_fields in engine/storage/inspect.py — those three plus the MetaPage dataclass are the whole change surface.

An event dataclass field named `level` or `category` SILENTLY COLLIDES with DiagnosticEvent's ClassVars: re-annotating a ClassVar as an instance field makes dataclass build a broken __init__ ('non-default argument follows default argument'). Index events use `tree_level` for this reason.

Page.insert_at / delete_at RENUMBER slots. Correct for index pages (nothing outside holds an index slot id), catastrophic for heaps (every RecordId would move). Never call them from heap.py. PostgreSQL draws the same line with PageIndexTupleDelete.

Database.insert_many / delete now walk every index on the table, so an insert emits catalog lookups and a chendb_indexes heap scan before the first RecordInsertedEvent. Tests counting the first N events off the WS must filter by event_type — see drain_events(of_type=...) in tests/integration/test_websocket.py.

Database.delete has to READ the row before deleting it, because an index entry is keyed on the value. That is why a delete costs a read even when the caller knows the address, and why PostgreSQL defers index cleanup to VACUUM instead.

create_index populates the tree BEFORE inserting the chendb_indexes row, so root splits during the build are already reflected in the root_page written. The on_root_changed callback is attached only afterwards, for later splits.

The CLI (python -m engine) had NO tests and was broken from M4 through M5 — db.table and db.schema became a method and a removed attribute. tests/integration/test_cli.py now covers every command. Keep it that way: it is one of the three promised usage modes.

examples/milestone1_storage.py was also broken by M4's table-scoped API and is fixed. Nothing runs the examples in CI; check them by hand after an API change: for f in examples/milestone*.py; do .venv/bin/python "$f" >/dev/null || echo FAIL $f; done

A rewrite rule must return the SAME OBJECT when it changes nothing, or apply_rules reports it as having fired on every query. fold_constants originally rebuilt every BinaryOp unconditionally and the 'rewrites applied' list became noise. See fold_constants_in in engine/optimizer/rules.py.

`-100` parses as UnaryOp(NEGATE, Literal(100)), not a negative literal, so `col < -100` matches neither the selectivity estimator's nor the index planner's `column <op> literal` shape until constant folding collapses it. Fold before estimating — see selectivity_of() in tests/unit/test_cost_model.py.

Charging CPU_TUPLE_COST for predicate evaluation double-counts the decode and over-costs a filtered sequential scan by 45%, which biases every crossover toward the index. CPU_PREDICATE_COST exists for this. If you add an operator, check the us-per-cost-unit column in benchmarks/index_vs_scan.py stays flat.
ANALYZE (gather statistics) and EXPLAIN ANALYZE (run the query, report actual rows) do opposite things and share a word. Both exist; do not conflate them.

The API caps a response at DEFAULT_MAX_ROWS = 10,000. A benchmark or test measuring a predicate matching more must pass max_rows, or the measurement stops early while the estimate covers the whole predicate — which makes a correct cost model look like it over-estimates by 40%.

Operator ids are numbered PER TYPE (filter_1, project_1), not globally. A shared counter produced project_2 for the first project and broke several step-mode tests. See _Namer in engine/planner/physical.py.

PlanTree and PlanPanel are different components. Adding something to PlanPanel does NOT make it appear in the Execution workspace, which renders PlanTree directly — the alternatives section had to be wired into both.

PagerStats.page_reads is LOGICAL from Milestone 7 (times the engine asked); physical_reads is syscalls. Tests asserting page_reads as a proxy for I/O now measure logical reads — usually what they meant, but check.

tests/integration/test_websocket.py's drain_events(until=N) BLOCKS FOREVER if N exceeds the connection's queue capacity: a burst happens inside one request, so every event is offered before the loop runs and all but the newest queue_size are dropped. Adding BufferPoolEvent pushed a test past the ceiling and hung the suite. Keep `until` under websocket_queue_size.

A table smaller than the pool never evicts, so a test or example that wants to show eviction must either seed past the capacity or open with buffer_pool_frames=<small>. Database.open takes that parameter for this reason.

Every INSERT through the API ends in a sync, which flushes the pool — so the dirty frame count is normally 0 in API tests. That is the durability contract holding, not the pool failing to buffer. Assert on writes_absorbed instead.
engine/transaction/manager.py: TransactionState.FAILED is open-but-doomed. `is_finished` is `not is_open`, so FAILED counts as open. Anything switching on state must handle four values, not three.

Pager._write_at takes `capture=False` for two callers: allocating a brand-new page (it is not in the file yet, so reading it to snapshot raises 'short read') and restore_page during a rollback (it would try to capture the page it is restoring).

Database.rollback() must reload the meta page and invalidate the catalog AND statistics caches. Restoring bytes is not enough — a rolled-back CREATE TABLE otherwise leaves the engine serving a table whose heap page was overwritten.

MILESTONE is now derived: engine/__init__.py computes it from __version__'s minor number, and engine/server/app.py re-exports it. Bumping the version in engine/__init__.py AND pyproject.toml is the whole job; tests/unit/test_architecture_boundaries.py pins all three together. The CLI banner sat a whole milestone behind before this.
MILESTONE_FEATURES must gain one entry per milestone or test_the_feature_list_has_one_entry_per_milestone fails.

PRIMARY KEY is metadata only — uniqueness is enforced by a UNIQUE index, which a table may not have. Any demo or test relying on a duplicate-key failure must create the index first, or it silently succeeds.

The repo is NOT `ruff format` clean at its configured line-length = 92 (43 files would reformat). `make lint` runs `ruff check` only, so nothing catches it. Running `ruff format` over the whole tree adds ~70 files of churn to a diff — format only the files you actually touched.

An LSN is a BYTE OFFSET in the log stream, not a counter. Two consequences: 'durable up to LSN n' is a comparison, and log.next_lsn is readable before appending — which the pager needs, because the page inside a record has to carry that record's LSN.

read_page_lsn returns -1 for an absent page, NEVER 0. Zero is a real LSN (the first record ever written, which for a new database is the meta page), and conflating them makes redo skip it. A unit test against a dictionary found this.
The meta page has its own LSN stamper: stamp_meta_lsn (offset 60, checksum at 80). Using engine.storage.page.stamp_lsn on page 0 writes a u64 over format_version and a u32 over the magic.

Checkpoint order is flush pages -> fsync db -> append CHECKPOINT -> fsync log -> write meta DIRECTLY (around the log and the pool) -> truncate. The direct write is unavoidable: logging it would put a record in the log about to be truncated. A crash between the meta write and the truncate is safe because decode_record rejects a record whose stored LSN does not match its position.

WAL record coalescing only applies to the immediately preceding STAGED record. Once flushed, a page carrying that LSN may be on disk and rewriting the record behind it would desynchronise them. This optimisation is the difference between a 197x and a 5x log.

UndoLog.capture marks a page captured even when it has no room for the bytes. First-write-wins is a DECISION, and the WAL asks the same question through has(). Letting it lapse made the log record mid-transaction states each claiming to be the rollback target.
Pager.abandon() / Database.abandon() / Workspace.crash() lose data on purpose — they are the crash button. Never call them from a normal path.

The direct Python API (db.insert, db.create_table) does NOT open an implicit transaction; only the SQL layer does. So a bare db.insert() is not committed and not durable until sync(). engine/database.py's docstring says so.

Rows carry an 8-byte tuple header (xmin u32, xmax u32) BEFORE the null bitmap. Anything that reads a heap payload must strip_tuple_header() before decode_record(). Missing one produces 'record has N trailing bytes after decoding K columns' — that message means a missed strip, not a schema problem.

The catalog's own tables carry NO tuple header and are not versioned; Database.scan branches on info.is_system. A rolled-back CREATE TABLE is undone by restoring the page, so there is never a catalog row anybody wants an older version of.

read_page_lsn / snapshot horizons: 0 is a REAL transaction id boundary. meta.next_xid becomes frozen_xid on open, and a row with xmin >= that is invisible. If rows vanish after a reopen, next_xid was not persisted — it is stamped by Pager.on_checkpoint, which Database sets to _stamp_next_xid.
UndoLog.capture and the MVCC first-write-wins rule share the same `_captured` set. Marking a page captured must not depend on there being room for its bytes.

A delete no longer tombstones: it rewrites xmax in place via Page.overwrite, which REFUSES anything but an equal-length write because a record that changed size would have to move and invalidate every index entry pointing at its record id.

Database.in_session(name) swaps the current session for a block. The pager's on_before_write hook reads self._session lazily for exactly this reason — binding it at construction would freeze the session.
MILESTONE is major * 10 + minor, because 1.0.0 is Milestone 10 and there is no 0.10.0 that sorts after 0.9.0.
The lock manager's victim is the YOUNGEST transaction, and the victim is the one that raises — not the detector. Changing that would make the loser depend on thread scheduling.

`make lint` runs `ruff check` AND `ruff format --check`. Both have been in the target since Milestone 1, and the format half was red from Milestone 1 to Milestone 10 — unnoticed because everything was verified by running `ruff check` directly, which was always green. The linter and the formatter are separate tools. Run `make lint`, not `ruff check`.

Format only the files you touched. A whole-tree `ruff format` used to add ~44 files of reflow to any diff; the tree is clean now, so it should stay a no-op, but a version bump of ruff could change that.

The visualizer's 'try it' and 'walkthrough' buttons build real SQL and no test checks that it parses. One shipped broken (see known_issues). Two earlier ones shipped with hardcoded column counts that broke on a three-column table, which is why visualizer/src/lib/demoRows.ts exists — build demo SQL from the table's real schema, never from an assumption.

SQL DML is INSERT only. UPDATE, DELETE and DROP are refused by engine/parser/parser.py:_NOT_YET. Database.delete(table, record_id) and the HTTP delete-record endpoint work — the gap is the SQL surface, not the engine.

Bumping engine.__version__ changes docs/openapi.json (FastAPI puts the version in the info block). Run `make types` in the SAME commit or CI's freshness check fails — this is exactly what CI caught on its first run.

Database.transaction() and execute_script() must use Database.active_transaction (session-aware), NEVER TransactionManager.active (default session only). Getting it wrong leaves a named session's implicit transaction open forever: the write reports success and stays invisible to everyone.

A writer must not skip a row just because header.deleted is set. Ask whether the transaction in xmax has FINISHED (not in running_ids). Still open means it may yet roll back, so take the lock and block. Database._claim_row is the only place this belongs.
UPDATE and DELETE materialise their matched rows before writing (_locate_rows). Removing that reintroduces the Halloween problem; tests/unit/test_dml.py catches it.

Demo SQL goes in visualizer/src/lib/demoSql.ts, never inline in a component, and is built from the open table via demoRows.ts. tests/integration/test_demo_sql.py runs every entry against a real engine.

scripts/emit_demo_sql.ts runs under plain Node type stripping: value imports in demoSql.ts need an explicit .ts extension (allowImportingTsExtensions is on), type-only imports are erased and may use the @/ alias.
MILESTONE_FEATURES may lag MILESTONE by one. Milestone 12 added CI, which is not something the engine can do, so it has 11 entries at MILESTONE 12.

Two browser consoles cannot demonstrate a write-write conflict: ManagedDatabase holds one RLock per request, so locate-and-mutate is atomic across consoles and a row-lock wait would deadlock against the engine lock. Asserted in tests/unit/test_mvcc.py instead.

A bound column index addresses the JOINED row, whose layout is the order the tables were WRITTEN in and never changes however the planner reorders. Anything that needs a column's position within its own table uses BoundColumnRef.table_position — statistics lookups especially. Getting that wrong collapses selectivity estimates silently.

Below the topmost join every row is the full width of the FROM. A join merges by copying the right side's slices into the left's row — never by 'take whichever side is not None', because a genuine SQL NULL is indistinguishable from an empty slot.

Aggregate names (COUNT, SUM, AVG, MIN, MAX) are deliberately NOT reserved words. They are parsed as an identifier followed by '(' so `count` stays usable as a column name, which is what PostgreSQL and SQLite do.

After a HashAggregate the row is [group keys..., aggregates...] and the binder rewrites every projection to index into THAT, reusing BoundColumnRef. The expression evaluator needed no change; do not invent a new node type for it.
engine/executor/operators.py must not import from engine/planner/*. RowLayout lives in engine/executor/binder.py beside Scope for that reason.
Implementing a SQL feature makes any demo or example that claims it is unsupported go stale. `make ci` catches it — it happened twice in Milestone 13 for ORDER BY.

The API has NO authentication and no disk quota. max_open_databases / max_rows_per_query / max_page_bytes_returned cap responses, not writes. Never expose the server on a public URL without building per-visitor workspaces, a reaper and a quota first. A tailnet or localhost is fine.
FastAPI runs `def` route handlers in a worker thread. That is invisible on a real server and fatal under WASM. If you ever wonder why the browser build has a threadpool shim, this is why.
Vercel Root Directory must stay at the REPO ROOT. bundle-engine.mjs reads ../engine, so pointing it at visualizer/ breaks the build.

User-facing text must never say a feature is missing. Six strings did, for up to thirteen milestones. visualizer/src/test/uiText.test.ts strips comments and then fails on milestone-deferral or shipped-subsystem-absent claims — a comment explaining history is fine, the same sentence in a title= is a lie. Describe what a thing does, or use the /health feature flag.

Never hardcode a value the engine can report. The access-path badge was the literal string 'seq scan' from Milestone 3 to 16, so every index scan from Milestone 5 on was mislabelled — persuasively, by naming a real access path with confidence.

The guards work only over what they enumerate. Milestone 12's covers SQL in demoSql.ts; two of the six stale strings were not SQL. uiText.test.ts covers source prose; it cannot catch a wrong NUMBER, only wrong words.

clearStoredData() deletes the IndexedDB database IDBFS is mounted over. RELOAD IMMEDIATELY AFTER. Clearing and carrying on leaves the mount pointing at nothing: in-memory files remain so the session looks fine, and the next sync writes into a recreated store. This made persistence look broken when it was not.
Never end a persistence path with .catch(() => {}). A silent sync failure is indistinguishable from nothing having been written, which cost three rounds of debugging in Milestone 16.

The browser build's format stamp uses FORMAT_VERSION (engine/storage/constants.py), not engine.__version__. Bumping the engine version must NOT clear a visitor's databases; only a file-format change should.

A GUARD CAN AGREE WITH A BUG. tests/unit/test_expression.py had `assert is_true(1) is False, "a truthy non-boolean must not pass"`. The comment is right — Python truthiness must not leak into SQL — and the assertion was one step short: 'not passing' and 'being rejected' are the same thing to a Filter, so WHERE v over an INTEGER matched nothing silently. When a differential failure points at code that already has a test, read the test before trusting it.

canonical() in tests/differential/dialect.py MUST NOT separate two values that values_agree() calls equal. It did: repr(-0.0) != repr(0.0) while -0.0 == 0.0, so a tie run containing `a.f * 0.0` grouped differently for the two engines and the oracle reported three divergences against a correct engine. A comparison key finer than the equality it serves invents differences. There is a test for the invariant.

total_order in the differential generator needs a unique non-null key from EVERY source, not just one. A primary key is unique in its own table, not in a join's output — a self-join ordered by b.pid repeats every key — and calling that total made the tester report two legal tie orders as a divergence. Expr.owner exists for this.

NEVER put BEGIN/ROLLBACK inside a single execute_script() call. The whole script runs in one implicit transaction and BEGIN *adopts* it rather than nesting, so a ROLLBACK discards the CREATE TABLE that came earlier in the same script. Documented at engine/executor/engine.py:1223 and deliberate; a probe agent reported it as a bug. Separate calls behave correctly. tests/differential/engines.py runs setup and each query as separate calls for exactly this reason.

An outer join's ON must never enter plan_select's conjunct pool. The pool is what lets a condition be pushed down to a scan or become a join key, and both are wrong for an outer join: `ON a.id = b.id AND b.y > 5` keeps every row of a, while the same predicate in the WHERE throws the NULL-extended ones away. _plan_joins takes the written-order steps so it can tell which is which.

preserve_left/preserve_right on a PhysicalJoin describe the PHYSICAL inputs, not the LEFT or RIGHT in the query. That is what lets the planner still choose a build side for an outer join: swap the inputs, flip the flags, identical output row — because RowLayout fixes every column's position by written order. If you ever make the planner swap an outer join's sides, the flags must swap with them.

HashJoin: 'is the bucket empty' and 'did this row match' are DIFFERENT QUESTIONS. A probe row can hash into a full bucket and be rejected by the residual for every candidate in it — `ON a.id = b.id AND b.y > 0` — and such a row is unmatched. Emitting only on an empty bucket lost rows from FULL JOIN. Nine hand-written cases missed it; the generator found it because a third of its outer joins carry an extra ON term.

HashJoin's buckets hold INDICES into self._build, not rows, and _build_matched is set[int] not set[Row]. Two identical build rows are two rows; a set of row values would treat them as one and an unmatched duplicate would go missing from a LEFT join. Same reason NestedLoopJoin tracks _right_matched by index.

A NULL-keyed row stays out of the hash table (NULL = NULL is UNKNOWN) and stays IN the build list. It cannot match, which for a preserved side is precisely why it must be emitted. The pre-M18 comment 'dropped from both sides' is now only true of an inner join.

_bounds_for must INTERSECT an equality with the existing bounds, not assign low = high = key. Assigning made `WHERE id = 3 AND id = 2` fold to `id = 2` with BOTH conjuncts marked absorbed, so id = 3 was dropped and the query returned a row. Unsatisfiable predicates are what a generated query produces constantly. Latent until PRIMARY KEY gave id an index — a fix in one place made a bug in another reachable.

_bounds_for must not absorb a predicate whose literal does not round-trip through the index key encoding. encode_key(v, FLOAT) does float(v), so `f = 9223372036854775807` rounds UP to 2^63 — and the index answered `=` with the row a seq scan excludes and `>` by excluding the row a scan returns. Both inverted, and only when an index happened to exist.

FLOAT means a FINITE double since M17, like INTEGER means exactly int64. NaN and inf were storable and IEEE comparison is a PARTIAL order: ORDER BY came back genuinely unsorted, MIN/MAX never displaced their seed, and index/key.py orders NaN above +inf while the evaluator says NaN > 398.0 is false. PostgreSQL instead defines a total order over them — that is four coordinated changes (comparison, sort, the aggregates, the key encoding), which is why refusing was chosen.

check_numeric_range() guards every arithmetic result, unary minus, division and SUM. The rule it enforces: an expression must not be able to produce a value a column of the same type would refuse. It could, in both directions.

SUM and AVG are refused over TEXT and BOOLEAN at BIND time (binder._require_aggregable). MIN/MAX deliberately still take anything — they only compare and return an input, so they are total on every type ChenDB has. PostgreSQL has no min(boolean); refusing it here would be strictness for its own sake.

The demo catalogue's 'Not implemented yet' slot has had THREE occupants: ORDER BY until M13, LEFT JOIN until M18, DISTINCT now. It has caught its own staleness both times, on the first run after the feature shipped. examples/milestone2_parser.py has the same line in its 'errors carry a position' list and fails the same way in `make examples` on a bare interpreter. Expect to update both together.

A version bump needs FOUR edits plus a regeneration: engine/__init__.py __version__, pyproject.toml version, the milestone number in tests/integration/test_api.py, the README's CLI banner transcript (line ~75, which is literal and must match ' + '.join(MILESTONE_FEATURES)) — then `make types` in the SAME commit, because info.version changes docs/openapi.json and CI diffs the committed copy.

A DOCSTRING under engine/server/ is API documentation. Pydantic uses a model's docstring as its JSON-schema description and FastAPI uses a route function's docstring as the operation description, so rewording either moves docs/openapi.json and CI fails with 'api.ts is stale'. Run `make types` in the same commit. `make ci` now catches this locally; before that it did not, while its own comment claimed it ran everything CI runs.

A STALE __pycache__ can make scripts/generate_api_types.py emit a docstring whose source file has already been reverted. It looks exactly like the generator ignoring its input. `find . -name __pycache__ -not -path './.venv/*' -prune -exec rm -rf {} +`.

The em-dash sweep was wrong four times before it was right, and each way was invisible until looked for. (1) Its 'is this a literal' guard looked for a quote NEAR the dash rather than AROUND it, so every `— \`code\`` was skipped, and this codebase writes that constantly. (2) `| — |` placeholders in markdown tables became `|, |`. (3) In an ALIGNED ASCII listing the dash is a COLUMN SEPARATOR, so a comma reads as prose; engine/errors.py's exception tree and docs/architecture.md's file map want colons. (4) Worst: a BORDERED table mock in docs/milestone-09-wal.md had its placeholder dashes paired into parentheses ACROSS rows, wrecking the column alignment. Any bordered diagram row must be restored byte for byte. If a similar sweep is ever needed, check all four.

The README's CLI transcript is verified by RE-RUNNING it, never from memory. Two of its lines were false: `.tree users_age` printed `root page 5` when it is page 6 (Milestone 17's implied primary-key index took page 5), and the plan claimed `IndexScan` when the real plan is a `SeqScan` (two rows fit in one page, so the cost model turns the index down). The transcript now shows the seq scan and explains why, because a fabricated IndexScan is worse than an honest scan.

A PRIMARY KEY now creates <table>_pkey, which means it OCCUPIES PAGES and shifts every page number after it. Any doc, transcript or test that pins a page id was written before Milestone 17 and may be off by one index's worth of pages.

An outer join's own ON is not evidence that the join can be simplified. `a LEFT JOIN b ON b.x = 5` cannot be TRUE about a NULL-extended row either, and rewriting on that basis is wrong, because an ON decides which rows MATCH and the non-matching rows are exactly what the join preserves. Treating an ON like a WHERE is the entire difference between the two clauses. tests/unit/test_joins.py::test_an_outer_joins_own_on_is_not_evidence_about_itself pins it.

preserves_left creates NULLs on the RIGHT. The rows a LEFT join keeps are the LEFT rows that found no partner, so it is the RIGHT side's columns that come back NULL. Every line of the simplification rule reads backwards from the naive expectation and that is not a typo.

match's literal patterns compare None/True/False by IDENTITY and everything else with ==, so `case Literal(value=True)` does NOT match Literal(1). nullability.py spells it `Literal(value=bool() as value)` anyway, because soundness-critical code should not depend on remembering that rule.

join_selectivity took ROW COUNTS where the textbook formula wants DISTINCT COUNTS, and a foreign-key join came out at the size of the wrong side (80x low on 50 users to 4,000 orders). distinct_join_selectivity had the right formula since Milestone 6 and nothing called it. If a plan looks oddly cheap above a join, check what the join itself estimated first: the error compounds upward, so 80x on two tables is 6,400x on three.

`make types-check` runs `git diff --exit-code`, so it fails on an UNCOMMITTED regeneration even when you have just run `make types` correctly. Commit, then re-run `make ci`. In CI the tree is clean at HEAD so the check means what it says.

The version bump alone moves docs/openapi.json (the OpenAPI `info.version` is engine.__version__), so every milestone needs `make types` in the same commit, not only the ones that touch a docstring under engine/server/.

A rewrite rule that fires too eagerly does not crash. It returns FEWER ROWS, quietly, and nothing downstream would attribute the loss to the optimiser. So the tests for one are weighted at when it must NOT fire (nine of Milestone 19's twenty-six join cases), and the rule is also run against itself with the rule removed from RULES so every answer has to be identical.

STATISTICS_TARGET = 32 is the boundary between an estimate and a count. A column at 32 distinct values or fewer has a COMPLETE most-common list and no histogram; one above it has 32 MCVs and buckets over the rest. Tests that want one regime or the other must be on the right side of 32, and a test fixture that drifts across the boundary changes which code path it exercises.

Counter.most_common breaks ties by INSERTION order, which for a statistics gather is heap order. A plan that depended on it would be planned differently after a VACUUM. summarise() sorts by (-count, value) instead, and tests/unit/test_cost_model.py pins it.

execute_script stops at DEFAULT_MAX_ROWS = 10,000 (engine/executor/engine.py). Measuring actual row counts with len(result.rows) therefore silently compares against 10,000 on any query bigger than that. The skewed join in tests/unit/test_estimates.py returns 5.8 million and briefly looked like a 581x estimation error because of it. Use SELECT COUNT(*).

A cost-model change is verified by the differential suite for the thing it must NOT do (change an answer) and by tests/unit/test_estimates.py for the thing it must (be closer to the truth). Neither alone is enough: the fuzzer cannot see a bad estimate and the estimate suite cannot see a wrong row.

`<` and `<=` used to produce identical estimates, because a straight line from min to max cannot resolve a single value. They now differ by the equality estimate added on top, which is what PostgreSQL does (scalarltsel against scalarlesel) and which slightly double-counts against the histogram's within-bucket interpolation. Accepted.

TWO TABLES WAS NOT ENOUGH, twice. The differential generator built parent and child for four milestones and found seven bugs; the day it grew a grandchild it found two more within minutes, both shipped wrong answers. Neither is expressible with two tables: one needs a join AFTER an outer join, the other an inner ON BELOW one. If a planner change looks untested, ask how many tables the corpus builds before believing the green.

The differential shrinker re-runs the same case in the same workspace directory, so anything keyed on the seed alone collides with the previous attempt. chendb_outcomes deletes case<seed>.chendb* before opening. A shrink report reading 'the generated setup does not apply' means this broke again, not that the schema is bad.

MINIMUM_SQLITE_VERSION has to move when the generator learns new syntax. It sat at 3.30 (NULLS LAST) for three milestones after Milestone 18 started emitting RIGHT and FULL JOIN, which need 3.39. The guard passed and the campaign would have died on a syntax error.

_search_join_order's DP table is keyed by which INPUTS a subplan covers, not which tables. The two are the same only when every input is a single table, which stops being true the moment an outer join hands the search a relation holding several. Keying by tables silently dropped every table joined after an outer join from the plan.

execute_script stops at DEFAULT_MAX_ROWS = 10,000, and that has now bitten twice. Comparing two PLANS by their returned rows on a query bigger than the cap compares two different prefixes and looks exactly like a reordering that changed the answer. Keep such fixtures under the cap or compare COUNT(*).

min_left is computed from the outer join's ON ALONE. An empty intersection with the syntactic left falls back to the syntactic left, because an ON that reads nothing there has proved nothing. Shrinking it further using the WHERE (which PostgreSQL does) would recover more orderings and needs its own argument.

test_layout.conftest: tests/conftest.py has db_path, users_schema, sample_rows, pager, sink, tracer, db fixtures; TINY_PAGE_SIZE = 256.
test_layout.btree_tests: tests/unit/test_bplustree.py uses TINY_PAGE_SIZE = 256 so a handful of keys forces a split, and every mutating test ends in tree.verify(), which asserts the WHOLE structure (sorted nodes, separators bounding their subtrees, all leaves at one depth, the sibling chain in order). Sampled lookups are not enough evidence: a split that promotes the wrong key still answers most queries correctly.
test_layout.planner_tests: tests/unit/test_cost_model.py's crossover tests are the ones that matter: they pin down where the index stops paying, and fail if a change to the constants moves it. The boundaries came from benchmarks/index_vs_scan.py.
test_layout.tests/differential/: Milestone 17. Generative differential testing against SQLite. One test per seed (CI_SEEDS = range(64)); CHENDB_DIFFERENTIAL_SEEDS='0:5000' widens it without a code change. test_harness.py is the part that stops the suite going quiet — a coverage floor over 23 named corners, a non-triviality floor, and a planted difference of every kind the oracle claims to detect. test_registry.py enforces the five constraints on what may be registered and re-runs every entry's minimal example. No new pytest marker: the long run is a script, not a test.

backlog.why: PostgreSQL's min_lefthand/min_righthand per SpecialJoinInfo, so the search can PROVE a reordering safe by set containment instead of assuming it is not, plus the identity-2 and identity-3 rules for when an outer and an inner join do commute. Milestone 19 took the common case off this pile by proving many outer joins away entirely, and it also fixed the join estimate, so extra freedom is now freedom the search can use.

Milestone 19 fixed join_selectivity to divide by distinct values rather than row counts, which was wrong by 80x on a foreign-key join. distinct_count is still ONE number and skew defeats it: ten million orders spread over three customers is distinct = 3, and the estimate is off by six orders of magnitude. An MCV list plus a histogram is the standard answer and the single largest thing missing from this cost model.

tailscale up, bind the server, systemd unit. A tailnet IS the auth: the API has none, so it must never be public. Buys real fsync, the recovery suite forking and SIGKILLing processes, and benchmarks off the laptop.

backlog.item: Smaller, named in the milestone docs
backlog.why: USING and NATURAL JOIN (both need the binder to merge two columns into one output column, which the flat RowLayout cannot express); GROUP BY ordinals (ORDER BY has them, GROUP BY silently treats an integer literal as a grouping constant, refusing it is the honest minimum); ORDER BY on an expression outside the select list (ChenDB sorts above the projection); RETURNING and INSERT ... SELECT (one refactor covers the pair); heap-only tuples; TRUNCATE; a coverage gate; a Python version matrix; SharedArrayBuffer for real threads and therefore step mode in the browser.

wasm_spike.verdict: PASSES. The unmodified engine runs under Pyodide and answers in-process ASGI calls.
wasm_spike.ran: scripts-free spike under Node with pyodide 314.0.3; engine/*.py copied into MEMFS, no host filesystem mount.

versions.pydantic: 2.12.5 with pydantic_core 2.41.5 — the Rust core has a wasm32 wheel and really validates

proved: CREATE TABLE / INSERT write real pages; page 4 reports HEAP, owner users, checksum_valid true, LSN 82668
A join + GROUP BY + HAVING + ORDER BY returns the CORRECT rows
EXPLAIN shows PhysicalHashJoin — the Milestone 13 planner works in WASM
The crash button works: abandon, reopen, recovery replays 24 records over 4 finished transactions, and the committed row survives
os.fsync does not raise on MEMFS (but has nothing to sync to, so it is not durability)
wasm_spike.the_one_blocker: RuntimeError: can't start new thread. FastAPI offloads SYNCHRONOUS route handlers to a worker thread via anyio.to_thread.run_sync, and WASM has no threads. Every ChenDB router is `def`, not `async def`. Fixed with a ~6-line BROWSER-ONLY shim that patches anyio.to_thread.run_sync and starlette.concurrency.run_in_threadpool to run inline. ZERO engine changes. Do NOT 'fix' this by making the routers async def: that would serialise the real server across databases too.
wasm_spike.architecture_decision: Because the ASGI app runs in-process, the browser build reuses the SAME routers, mappers, Pydantic models and error envelope. No engine/server/browser.py, no duplicated endpoint layer, no drift guard needed, and api.ts stays generated from the one OpenAPI schema.
still_unknown: Step mode is dead in-tab and this is confirmed, not guessed: StepController blocks a thread. It ships disabled behind the existing /health features flag.
